background.definition: Urinary retention is a set of symptoms characterized by complete cessation of urination or the inability to empty the bladder completely.

list.listitem: In a prospective cohort study of male health professionals between the ages of 45 and 83 years without a history of prostate cancer or surgery, the incidence was 4.5 per 1000 per year, between the ages of 40 and 83 years.
Incidence was higher in men with worse symptoms, but even in those at highest risk (AUA symptom score >8 and known BPH), the annual incidence was only 14 per 1000 person per years.
Women: not well documented in the literature.
In an analysis of men with benign prostatic hypertrophy enrolled in the placebo group of clinical trials, the risk of AUR was approximately 1% per year.
In more than half of men with urinary retention, it is caused by benign prostatic hypertrophy.
Other causes include prostate cancer, urethral stricture, postoperative complications, neurologic disorders, medications, and urinary tract Infection.
In women, pregnancy can also cause urinary retention secondary to an obstructing uterus.
Pathophysiologic mechanisms differ depending on the etiology. In general, three factors predominate and often overlap: outflow obstruction, neurologic impairment, and overdistension.
In men with moderate to severe BPH, finasteride 5 mg daily prevents the development of AUR (NNT = 25 for 4 years). B
The best predictors of AUR are a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying, weak urinary stream, having to void again after <2 hours, and use of adrenergic or anticholinergic medications. C
If urinary retention is suspected, catheterization and measurement of postvoid residual (PVR) volume will confirm retention. C
History and physical should focus on determining the etiology of urinary retention to treat the underlying disorder. C
Order BUN and serum creatinine to assess renal function, renal ultrasound to evaluate for hydronephrosis, and consider other imaging studies to rule out secondary causes such as malignancy. C

list.listitem: The best predictors of AUR are a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying, weak urinary stream, having to void again after <2 hours, and use of adrenergic or anticholinergic medications.

Establish the onset and duration of symptoms via history. AUR needs immediate treatment and evaluation for underlying disorders. Chronic urinary retention is not a medical emergency, but should be worked up and treated as an outpatient.
Many patients with AUR are in considerable distress. Along with the inability to pass urine, patients often experience lower abdominal and/or suprapubic discomfort.
Symptoms may be less pronounced when AUR is superimposed upon chronic urinary retention. Chronic urinary retention is most often painless.

Palpate and percuss the lower abdomen. The urinary bladder may be palpable, either on abdominal or rectal examination. The abdomen will sound dull on percussion. Deep suprapubic palpation will provoke discomfort. The patient should also be assessed for tenderness over the costovertebral angle, which may signal secondary hydronephrosis or pyeloneprhitis.
Perform a rectal examination to evaluate for masses, fecal impaction, and perineal sensation. A normal prostate examination does not preclude prostatic hypertrophy as a cause of obstruction.
In women, consider a pelvic examination to help confirm a distended bladder and diagnose gynecological masses or organ prolapse as a cause of obstruction.
Neurologic evaluation of strength, sensation, reflexes, and muscle tone of lower extremities may help to diagnose underlying disorders such as spinal cord compression or multiple sclerosis.

PVR bladder ultrasonography: Greater than 100 mL is abnormal and greater than 200 mL requires treatment. In women, symptoms are poor predictors of the PVR; increasing age and prolapse ≥Stage III predict greater PVR.
Other imaging studies may be indicated to find the cause of urinary retention (eg, abdominal/pelvis CT to evaluate for masses, MRI to detect spinal cord or brain tumors, multiple sclerosis).
Further tests may be helpful to evaluate sequelae of untreated urinary retention (eg, blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine for renal function, or renal ultrasound to evaluate for hydronephrosis).

Prostate specific antigen (PSA) predicts the likelihood of AUR in men with benign prostatic hypertrophy. In a study of over 3000 men who were in the placebo groups of clinical trials, PSA >3.0 ng/dL was 70% sensitive and 75% specific. Adding other clinical and laboratory variables did little to improve the ability to predict AUR. Since the baseline risk of AUR is low (about 1% per year), the predictive value of PSA >3.0 is also very low.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation and treatment.
In AUR, initiate rapid and complete bladder decompression using a Foley urethral catheter. Patients can then be followed by a trial without catheter. B
Suprapubic catheters improve patient comfort and decrease bacteriuria and recatheterization in patients requiring catheterization for up to 14 days. A
Silver alloy-impregnated urethral catheters reduce the incidence of urinary tract infections in hospitalized patients requiring catheterization for up to 14 days. A
Consider low-friction, hydrophilic-coated catheters for patients with neurogenic bladder who practice clean, intermittent self-catheterization. A
Medical treatment generally involves treatment of underlying causes, eg, benign prostatic hypertrophy, constipation, prostate cancer, urinary tract Infection, or urolithiasis.
Discontinue medications that may cause urinary retention (eg, sympathomimetics and medications with anticholinergic effects).
There is weak evidence to support the use of drugs to treat urinary retention after surgery.

To relieve discomfort of AUR, rapid and complete bladder decompression should be performed using a Foley urethral catheter. Gradual decompression is not effective in preventing complications associated with decompression.
After decompression of the bladder, about 80% will not need surgery in the 6 months after a trial without catheter.

Low-friction, hydrophilic-coated catheters increased patient satisfaction and decreased urinary tract infection and hematuria in patients with neurogenic bladder who practice clean, intermittent self-catheterization.
There is insufficient evidence regarding variables for intermittent catheterization including different designs, techniques, or catheterization strategies.

Placement of a suprapubic catheter is sometimes necessary in patients with urethral stricture disease, severe prostatic hypertrophy, or other anatomic abnormalities that preclude Foley catheter placement.
Suprapubic catheters improve patient comfort and decrease bacteriuria and recatheterization in patients requiring catheterization for up to 14 days.
Duration and method of treatment depends on underlying etiology.
Some patients with chronic retention may need indwelling catheters.
Hospitalization is indicated for patients who show signs of sepsis or have obstruction related to malignancy or spinal cord compression.
Silver alloy-impregnated urethral catheters reduce the incidence of urinary tract infections in hospitalized patients requiring catheterization for up to 14 days.
Untreated urinary retention can lead to detrusor muscle weakness and worsening of urinary retention. C
Untreated urinary retention can lead to hydronephrosis, which can then lead to chronic renal failure. C
After decompression of the bladder, about 80% will not need surgery in the 6 months after a trial without catheter. B
